title: The five Takhts
hook: the Ardas remembers the five seats of authority and all gurdwaras

segments.voice: Yesterday: for the gurdwaras, and your line: they kept the doors. Did a door you walked through remind you of who kept it open? Today the Ardas turns from people to places. Day six hundred twenty-six.
screen: `FOR THE GURDWARAS — THEY KEPT THE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Draw a map of India and put five pins in it. Two in Punjab, close together. One more in Punjab, farther south. One way out east, on the Ganges, in Bihar. And one deep in the south-center of the country, in Maharashtra, nearly a thousand miles from the others. A Sikh child in Toronto or Birmingham or Nairobi can usually name all five. They're not the biggest gurdwaras, or the most visited. They're something else: places where the community's authority sits. The Ardas names them, as a group, every time it's prayed. Today: the five Takhts.
screen: `FIVE PINS IN A MAP OF INDIA.` → `PUNJAB, BIHAR, MAHARASHTRA.` → `WHERE AUTHORITY SITS.`

segments.voice: After the martyrs, the Ardas says: panjaan takhtaan, sarbatt gurduaariaan daa dhiaan dhar ke. Fixing the mind on the five Takhts and all the gurdwaras, say Waheguru. Takht is a Persian word for a throne, the seat of a ruler. A gurdwara is a house of the Guru, where the sangat prays. A Takht is a seat of authority, where decisions for the whole community are made and announced. The first and best known is the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, which Guru Hargobind built facing the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar in 1606. We met it with his two swords. Edicts called hukamnamas, binding on Sikhs everywhere, are issued from there. The other four are tied to the life of Guru Gobind Singh. Takht Sri Patna Sahib, in Bihar, marks where he was born. Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, at Anandpur, marks where he founded the Khalsa in 1699. Takht Sri Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo in southern Punjab, is where tradition says he stayed in 1706 and a final edition of the scripture was prepared. And Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, at Nanded in Maharashtra, marks where he died in 1708. Damdama Sahib was formally recognized as the fifth Takht only in the twentieth century, so some older books list four. Then the Ardas widens out: sarbatt gurduaariaan, all the gurdwaras. Every one, from the Harmandir to a rented hall above a shop. Five seats of authority, and every house of the Guru: all held in mind in one breath.
screen: `TAKHT: A THRONE, A SEAT.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT, AMRITSAR, 1606.` · `FOUR SEATS FROM THE TENTH GURU'S LIFE.` · `AND ALL THE GURDWARAS.` · then, large: `FIVE SEATS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one Takht. Sit and breathe. Go through the five slowly in your mind: Akal Takht, Amritsar. Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur. Damdama Sahib, Talwandi Sabo. Patna Sahib, Bihar. Hazur Sahib, Nanded. Pick one, and picture it: its white or golden dome, the pilgrims, the morning light. Hold it for a few breaths. Then widen out to every gurdwara, including the one nearest you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Takht. A throne, a seat of authority: the Akal Takht and four seats from the life of Guru Gobind Singh.
Your line: five seats. Look up one Takht today, see where it sits on the map, and read one thing about it. Day six hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the five Takhts and all gurdwaras; hukamnamas for the whole community are issued from the Akal Takht in Amritsar.

fork.setup: a question comes up that affects Sikhs everywhere. where does tradition look for a hukamnama binding on the whole community?
fork.reveal: hukamnamas for the whole Panth are issued from the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, built by Guru Hargobind in 1606.

original.note: Gurmukhi: takht, a throne; from Persian, used for the five seats of Sikh authority.

trapdoor: what you thought: the five Takhts are the five holiest gurdwaras.
what it means: they're seats of authority, and the Ardas then remembers every gurdwara too.
what a scholar hears: the Akal Takht dates to 1606; Takht Sri Damdama Sahib was recognized as the fifth Takht by the SGPC in the 1960s.
